bills.title: Data center water reporting

recent_news.title: Virginia Lawmakers Pass 15 Data Center Bills as Tax Exemption Fight Looms
recent_news.takeaway: Both water reporting bills cleared the General Assembly and were sent to Gov. Spanberger with an April 13 deadline; final HB 496 requires utilities to report monthly aggregate water deliveries to data centers.

recent_news.title: Data center bills dominated this year's General Assembly. Here's what passed.
recent_news.takeaway: Conference committee produced parallel transparency tracks: HB 496 covers utility-side aggregate reporting while SB 553 lets localities require water estimates at rezoning.

recent_news.title: Bills on data center siting and water usage remain unresolved as General Assembly session winds down
recent_news.takeaway: Sen. Srinivasan called both bills 'transparency bills,' framing the conference committee fight as a question of which mechanism best surfaces data center water draws to the public.

Spanberger (D) ultimately signed both, with bipartisan votes in both chambers.

general_principles.note: Forces public visibility into water volumes data centers draw from municipal supplies, previously shielded as proprietary.

Lets localities weigh water consumption in special use permit and rezoning decisions for new facilities.

bills.title: Data center environmental, energy, and water requirements
bills.sponsor: Rep. Greg Davids
bills.summary: Water-appropriation permit process and DNR preapplication review for data centers expected to use >100M gal/yr; evaluates water source and conservation.
bills.status_detail: Signed by Gov. Walz June 14, 2025 (Laws 2025, 1st Spec. Sess., Ch. 12); amends Minn. Stat. 103G.271 / 103G.265.

recent_news.title: House OKs legislation to regulate data centers
recent_news.takeaway: House passed HF 16 85-43 during special session, coupling a 35-year sales tax exemption extension with new environmental guardrails on water and electricity.

recent_news.title: Lessons Learned for Data Center Regulation: A Conversation with Minnesota Advocates
recent_news.takeaway: Advocates reflect that the final bill paired environmental review thresholds (100M gallons/year) and demand fees ($2-5M/yr) with tax extensions opposed by progressives.

recent_news.title: What Minnesotans should learn about data centers
recent_news.takeaway: Sierra Club critiques HF 16 as insufficient, noting the bill extended lucrative sales tax breaks while only requiring pre-application water review above a high threshold (date approximated to month).

bills.public_sentiment: DFL-aligned environmental groups (Sierra Club North Star Chapter, Clean Water Action, Clean River Partners) opposed the package, arguing tax breaks for hyperscalers outweighed the environmental guardrails and that closed-loop cooling should have been mandated. Sponsor Rep. Greg Davids (R-Preston) and industry framed it as a 'jobs bill' protecting Minnesota's competitive position. Some DFL members like Rep. Acomb supported it as necessary guardrails; Rep. Hollins opposed it as 'tax breaks for billionaires.' Bipartisan deal-making in a divided legislature produced an uneasy compromise that no advocacy coalition celebrated.

general_principles.note: Triggers pre-application evaluation for facilities using more than 100 million gallons of water per year.
Imposes $2-5M annual fees tied to peak electricity demand to internalize grid impacts.
Advocates pushed (unsuccessfully) for mandates on water recycling; bill establishes review framework instead.
Couples water-use thresholds with clean energy tariff and sustainable design requirements.

bills.title: Data center water-use disclosure
bills.sponsor: Assemblymember Diane Papan (D–San Mateo)
bills.summary: Would have required data centers to disclose projected water use to their water supplier at business-license application and certify actual annual water use at license renewal.
bills.status_detail: Vetoed by Gov. Newsom on 2025-10-11, who cited an incomplete understanding of the impact on businesses and consumers. Would have required data centers to report expected water use to their supplier before applying for a business license, certify that disclosure at application, and certify actual annual use at renewal. recent_news.title: Governor Vetoes Papan Bill to Track Data Center Water Use
recent_news.takeaway: Papan rebuked the veto, calling AB 93 a 'reasonable, transparent approach' to documenting AI-era water demand that Newsom rejected as too rigid on industry.

recent_news.title: California Governor vetoes data center water use bill
recent_news.takeaway: Newsom's veto message said he was 'reluctant to impose rigid reporting requirements about operational details on this sector' without fuller impact analysis.

recent_news.title: Efforts to Regulate California Data Centers Falter — For Now
recent_news.takeaway: Industry attorneys note AB 93 was the modest survivor of a broader regulatory push, and even its disclosure framework was too much for the governor.

bills.public_sentiment: Backed by environmental and water-resource advocates and Assemblymember Diane Papan (D-San Mateo) as a transparency-first compromise after stricter proposals failed. The Data Center Coalition publicly opposed the bill, and tech industry groups warned the reporting regime would chill California investment relative to Texas, Virginia, and Arizona. Newsom sided with industry; Papan and water-policy advocates expressed frustration that even a modest disclosure framework couldn't survive, signaling broader CA reluctance to constrain AI infrastructure growth.

general_principles.note: Would have required water-use estimates at business licensing and annual self-certified actual-use reports at renewal.
Aimed to surface industry-wide water demand metrics that operators currently treat as proprietary.
Tied disclosure obligations to the local business license process rather than to environmental permitting.

Cleared the California State Legislature.

bills.title: Data Center Transparency Act
bills.sponsor: Sen. RaShaun Kemp (D-38) (lead); co-sponsors Anderson, Davenport, Echols

bills.status_detail: Read and referred to Senate Regulated Industries 2026-01-27; died at end of 2025-2026 biennium (sine die 2026-04-02) without crossover.

recent_news.title: Georgia lawmakers' failure to act on data center concerns draws community ire

recent_news.title: Bills to Protect Ratepayers From Data Centers Fail in Georgia Legislature
recent_news.takeaway: SB 421 was among the transparency measures that died without a hearing, leaving Georgia with no statutory mechanism to force disclosure of data center water and electricity use.

recent_news.title: Sen. RaShaun Kemp Introduces Legislation to Address Data Center Transparency
recent_news.takeaway: Kemp framed the bill around blocking NDAs that prevent the public from learning data center utility consumption, calling current secrecy 'alarming.'

bills.public_sentiment: Bipartisan sponsorship — Sen. RaShaun Kemp (D-Atlanta) joined by Sen. Drew Echols (R-49) — signaled rare cross-aisle alignment, with support from environmental and community groups (Science for Georgia, local residents fighting hyperscale projects in DeKalb and metro Atlanta). general_principles.note: Would have forced local governments to disclose water and electricity used by data center projects.
Core mechanism: bars counties and municipalities from signing nondisclosure agreements that hide utility consumption figures.
Targets the local-government side of secrecy rather than directly regulating data center operators.

Referred to committee; no hearing ever scheduled.

bills.title: Responsible Water Use by Data Centers Act
bills.sponsor: Sens. Willis Blackshear Jr. (D-Dayton) and Casey Weinstein (D-Hudson); co-sponsor Sen. Kent Smith (D-Euclid)
bills.summary: Makes data centers responsible for the water/sewer infrastructure costs they cause, requires a Division of Water Resources permit to consume water, and caps consumptive use at 5 MGD averaged over 30 days.
bills.status_detail: Introduced 2026-03-16; referred to Senate Public Utilities Committee.

recent_news.title: Lawmakers announce Ohio Joint Data Center Committee
recent_news.takeaway: Bipartisan legislators form joint committee to study data center impacts, signaling SB 378 is part of a broader regulatory push rather than an isolated effort.

recent_news.title: Ohio moves to ban data center construction through constitutional amendment as legislature introduces 4 regulatory bills in one week
recent_news.takeaway: SB 378 is grouped with three other bills (SB 374, SB 381, HB 784) as part of a coordinated legislative response to data center concerns; no hearings scheduled yet.

recent_news.title: Another Ohio bill looks to further regulate data centers, focusing on water usage
recent_news.takeaway: Outlines the 5 MGD/30-day cap and infrastructure cost-shift to data centers, framing the bill as protecting other ratepayers from subsidizing data center demand.

bills.public_sentiment: Support is concentrated among Ohio Senate Democrats (Blackshear, Weinstein, Smith, plus Minority Leader Antonio calling for bipartisan accountability) and grassroots groups like Save Ohio Parks active in opposing data center wastewater permits. Industry opposition has not yet been publicly voiced on SB 378 specifically, but the Data Center Coalition and major hyperscalers have historically resisted such caps. With Republicans controlling the Senate, the bill's path through the Public Utilities Committee is uncertain.

general_principles.note: Hard 5 MGD/30-day cap on consumptive water use, with permit suspension if violated.
Data centers must bear all water/sewer infrastructure costs they cause; protects existing ratepayers.
Requires permit from Division of Water Resources chief before consumptive withdrawal.

timeline.detail: Sponsored by Sens. Blackshear, Weinstein, Smith (all D).
Senate Public Utilities Committee.

bills.status_detail: Introduced in the 136th General Assembly; pending in House committee (House Technology & Innovation hearings referenced in late-2025 testimony).

recent_news.takeaway: Groups HB 784 with three Senate bills as a coordinated regulatory push; characterizes it as a basic reporting requirement compared to SB 378's hard caps.

recent_news.title: Ohio State Representatives introduce bill to track data center water usage
recent_news.takeaway: Cockley and Lett pitch the bill on transparency grounds, noting Ohio hosts 200+ data centers without statewide water reporting, and explicitly target NDA secrecy with municipalities.

Bars data centers from concealing water usage behind nondisclosure agreements with municipalities.
Public access to standardized water data for 200+ Ohio data centers that currently report nothing.

bills.title: South Carolina Data Center Responsibility Act
bills.sponsor: Reps. Cromer, Gilreath, Oremus, Chumley (plus co-sponsors)
bills.summary: Would require data centers to use closed-loop water/liquid cooling with zero net withdrawal and zero wastewater discharge, mandate annual third-party-verified certifications, and impose strict liability for environmental damage.

recent_news.takeaway: PMPA general manager Joel Ledbetter publicly dismisses H 4583 as probably 'not going anywhere,' while Westminster's Kevin Bronson backs softer 'guardrails' instead of energy-independence mandates.

recent_news.title: H 4583 introduced in South Carolina House
recent_news.takeaway: Rep. April Cromer (R-Anderson) and bipartisan co-sponsors file the most aggressive data center bill in the country: closed-loop cooling, zero discharge, energy independence, and strict liability.

bills.public_sentiment: Sponsored by a bipartisan but ideologically heterodox group led by Republican Rep. April Cromer (R-Anderson), with eight co-sponsors. Prohibits state or local taxpayer-funded incentives benefiting data centers.
Bans groundwater extraction and municipal water use for cooling; requires on-site power generation.

bills.status_detail: Amended in Assembly 2026-05-18 (prior amendments 2026-01-12, -03-26, -04-13); still pending in the Assembly.

recent_news.takeaway: 9-4 committee vote sends bill to Appropriations, signaling Democratic majority support but persistent Republican opposition.

recent_news.takeaway: Bauer-Kahan's prior bill AB 222 was gutted under Big Tech pressure (Silicon Valley Leadership Group, Data Center Coalition) and a related water-reporting bill was vetoed by Newsom, setting hostile precedent for AB 1577.

Companion bills (SB 761, 763) pair disclosure with withdrawal caps and ratepayer protections.
