recent_news.title: As Utility Costs Rise, Durbin Introduces New Legislation To Bring Transparency To Energy & Water Consumption By Data Centers
recent_news.takeaway: Original release: 5-year pre-construction projections, state-level reporting, EPA/DOE/USDA aggregated regional reports, and per-day fines for noncompliance.

bills.public_sentiment: Coverage aligns the bill with positions taken by Sierra Club Illinois, the Illinois Clean Jobs Coalition, and environmental advocates pushing parallel state-level transparency (Illinois POWER Act). The Data Center Coalition has opposed similar prescriptive transparency provisions in state legislation. Unlike the initial framing, S. 4213 drew bipartisan cosponsors, with reporting naming Sens. Josh Hawley (R-MO), Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), and Tom Cotton (R-AR).

general_principles.note: Mandates actual + 5-year projected energy and water consumption disclosure for new and existing facilities.
Requires pre-construction estimates so local governments can evaluate before approving facilities.
States aggregate and anonymize data for EPA, DOE, and USDA joint regional reports.
Frames disclosure as a response to data center demand driving up consumer utility costs.

timeline.detail: Sen. Dick Durbin (D-IL) introduced S. 4213; referred to committee.

bills.title: Large load interconnection, ERCOT oversight, and remote-disconnect
bills.sponsor: Sen. Phil King (R-Weatherford) lead; bipartisan co-authors
bills.summary: Imposes new planning, interconnection, and cost-recovery rules on large electric loads (≥75 MW) in ERCOT, including data centers. Requires backup-generation disclosure capable of meeting a share of site demand, mandates remote-disconnect capability for emergency load shedding, and forces disclosure of duplicative interconnection requests across utilities.
bills.status_detail: Signed by Gov. Abbott June 20, 2025 (89th Leg.); PUCT implementing rules proposed early 2026.

recent_news.title: Texas SB 6 Update: Proposed Interconnection Standards
recent_news.takeaway: PUCT proposed implementing rules early 2026; industry calls the curtailment clause the 'Kill Switch' provision.

recent_news.title: Texas law gives grid operator power to disconnect data centers during crisis
recent_news.takeaway: Abbott signature gives ERCOT first-in-nation authority to remotely curtail large loads during firm load shed.

bills.public_sentiment: Backed by Texas grid-reliability advocates, the PUCT, and a bipartisan supermajority citing Winter Storm Uri and AI-load growth. The Data Center Coalition and major hyperscalers lobbied to weaken the curtailment trigger and duplicate-request disclosure. Sierra Club Texas supported but called for parallel water rules. Texas Republican Party passed a 2026 resolution calling for further DC restrictions.

general_principles.note: Requires disclosure of duplicate interconnection requests and backup generation capacity.
Establishes that large loads pay for incremental transmission infrastructure costs.
PUCT gains expanded review authority over loads ≥75 MW.

timeline.milestone: Applies to all new large loads connecting after this date

bills.title: POWER Act (Protecting Oregonians With Energy Responsibility)
bills.sponsor: Rep. Pam Marsh (D-Ashland), lead; bipartisan co-sponsors
bills.summary: Creates a new utility customer classification for data centers, cryptocurrency operations, and other large industrial energy users (>20 MW). Requires them to pay their full share of electricity costs and transmission upgrades and to sign 10-year minimum-commitment contracts.
bills.status_detail: Signed by Gov. Kotek June 2025; OPUC adopted PGE implementation rules in early 2026.

recent_news.title: Oregon's POWER Act is the first of its kind to protect utility bills from data center growth
recent_news.takeaway: First-in-nation cost-allocation law specifically targeting large-load classification.

recent_news.title: Oregon Legislature passes 'POWER Act,' targeting industrial energy users like data centers
recent_news.takeaway: Bipartisan vote; legislative findings note a 30 MW DC consumes the same power as the City of Ashland.

bills.public_sentiment: Oregon CUB, Oregon Environmental Council, Climate Solutions, and the AFL-CIO building trades championed the bill. Pacific Power, PGE, and the Data Center Coalition initially opposed but negotiated softened language. The Dalles, Hillsboro, and Prineville residents — home to Google and Meta DCs — were active grassroots supporters.

general_principles.note: Forces large industrial loads (>20 MW) to bear their own grid expansion costs.
Requires DCs to disclose long-term load and contract terms to PUC.
10-year minimum commitment discourages speculative interconnection requests.

timeline.milestone: PGE implementation rules adopted by OPUC (approximate; Q1 2026)

bills.title: Data Center Water and Energy Usage Reporting Act
bills.sponsor: Sen. M. Teresa Ruiz (D-29); Sen. Raj Mukherji (D-32); co-sponsors Diegnan (D), Beach (D)
bills.summary: Requires data center owners/operators to submit semi-annual water and energy usage reports to the NJ Board of Public Utilities for three years. Reports must cover total kWh, IT-equipment energy, water input (cubic meters), and source. State-incentivized facilities must also report PUE, WUE, and renewable energy factor. BPU publishes facility data within 30 days; performance metrics released only in anonymized aggregated form (n≥5).
bills.status_detail: Passed Senate March 24, 2026; pending in Assembly committee. Governor's office signaled in May 2026 a preference for harder construction limits before signing.

recent_news.title: Legislation holding data centers accountable for water, energy use passes Senate
recent_news.takeaway: S3379 cleared NJ Senate as part of a three-bill package alongside clean-power and ratepayer-protection bills.

recent_news.title: Key Legislation to Ensure Data Center Transparency and Energy Affordability Moves Forward
recent_news.takeaway: Sierra Club, NJLCV, and Food & Water Watch built coalition support; bill emerged from committee with amendments.

bills.public_sentiment: Strongly supported by Sierra Club NJ, NJ League of Conservation Voters, Food & Water Watch, and South Jersey residents in Vineland, East Greenwich, and West Deptford fighting proposed DC projects. The Data Center Coalition and NJ Chamber of Commerce opposed, citing trade-secret concerns. Sen. Ruiz is the lead Latina state Senate champion. The Governor's office initially asked for revisions and as of late May 2026 is pushing for stronger construction limits before signing.

general_principles.note: Semi-annual BPU reporting forces public visibility into DC water and energy footprint.
Public posting of facility-level data within 30 days of submission.
Special PUE/WUE disclosure for state-incentivized facilities.

timeline.milestone: Governor calls for stronger construction limits

bills.title: New York State Sustainable Data Centers Act
bills.sponsor: Sen. Kristen Gonzalez (D-WF, 59th); Sen. Rachel May (D, 48th) co-sponsor; Assembly companion A9086 carried by Assm. Anna Kelles (D)
bills.summary: Requires data centers ≥5 MW to file pre-construction disclosure reports with the PSC covering location, labor, projected energy/water usage, waste heat, and water pollution. Mandates annual sustainability updates. Sets a renewable-energy schedule: 33% by 2030, 67% by 2035, 100% by 2040. Prohibits utility fossil-fuel PPA incentives and directs PSC to create a DC surcharge funding low- and moderate-income energy assistance in host communities.
bills.status_detail: Reported from Senate Energy and Telecommunications Committee in amended form (S6394A) May 19, 2025; carried over into 2026 session.

recent_news.title: How New York is responding to AI data center surge
recent_news.takeaway: S6394 is one of two flagship NY data center bills alongside S9144 moratorium.

recent_news.title: Sustainable Data Centers Act advances in NY Senate Energy Committee
recent_news.takeaway: Amended version cleared committee on party-line vote; carried over to 2026.

bills.public_sentiment: Backed by NRDC, NYLCV, NY Renews Coalition, and CLCPA implementation advocates. The Empire AI public research initiative would be exempt, securing university-system support. Major opposition from Data Center Coalition, NYISO market participants, and downstate utilities arguing the renewable mandate is technically unachievable. Sen. Gonzalez is a freshman DSA-aligned senator from Queens with industrial-district constituents.

general_principles.note: Pre-construction PSC disclosure of energy, water, and waste-heat projections.
Annual sustainability progress reports filed with PSC.
Progressive renewable mandate to 100% by 2040 aligned with CLCPA.
DC surcharge funds low-income energy assistance in host communities.

bills.title: Data Center Moratorium and PSC Rate Impact Review
bills.sponsor: Sen. Liz Krueger (D-28, Manhattan); Assm. Anna Kelles (D-125, Ithaca)
bills.summary: Imposes a moratorium of at least three years and ninety days on the issuance of permits for new private data centers ≥20 MW. Directs DEC to publish a generic environmental impact statement and PSC to issue orders minimizing rate impacts. Public-sector projects like the state's Empire AI research initiative are exempt.
bills.status_detail: Introduced February 2026; both pending in committee. In the session's final days the one-year Responsible Data Center Development Act (S10642/A11560, tracked separately) passed both chambers instead of this three-year version — re-verify whether S9144 remains a live separate vehicle in 2027 or was effectively superseded.

recent_news.title: Nearly 500 New York Small Businesses Back Moratorium Push on AI Data Centers
recent_news.takeaway: Small business coalition cites projected ~25% retail electricity price hike if hyperscale buildout proceeds without intervention.

recent_news.title: New York State Proposes Sweeping Data Center Moratorium and Regulatory Review (S9144)
recent_news.takeaway: Bill would block major hyperscale facilities while preserving Empire AI public research initiative.

bills.public_sentiment: Endorsed by NY Renews, Public Power NY, Sierra Club Atlantic Chapter, and consumer-rate advocates. The Taxpayers Protection Alliance named it 'Bill of Shame' for May 2026, and Data Center Coalition, NYC Partnership, and Greater NY Chamber are organized opponents. The Empire AI exemption is a deliberate carve-out from Sen. Krueger to preserve SUNY research while pausing private buildout.

general_principles.note: Hard pause on new private DC permits ≥20 MW for 3+ years.
DEC must issue generic EIS before moratorium lifts.
PSC ordered to minimize rate impact on residential/commercial users.

bills.title: Protecting Our Workers and Environment from Reckless Data Centers (POWER) Act
bills.sponsor: Sen. Ram Villivalam (D-8, Chicago); Rep. Robyn Gabel (D-18, Evanston)
bills.summary: Requires data centers to pay for their own energy infrastructure and invest in renewable generation, disclose annual water consumption (intake + discharge) to the Illinois DNR beginning Jan. 1, 2027, identify and monitor likely pollutants in discharges to WWTPs, ban NDAs between local governments and DC operators, and mandate transparent community-benefit agreements.
bills.status_detail: Introduced February 11, 2026 (Senate companion SB 4016); reported out of Senate Energy and Public Utilities Committee with amendments April 2026.

recent_news.title: Testimony in Support of POWER Act to Protect Illinois Water Resources from Data Center Impacts
recent_news.takeaway: Alliance highlighted Lake Michigan withdrawal compact obligations and the need to override NDAs hiding DC consumption.

recent_news.title: Illinois Legislators Introduce POWER Act, Which Would Force Data Centers To Foot Energy Costs
recent_news.takeaway: Bill makes Illinois the first state to explicitly ban municipal NDAs covering DC water and energy use.

bills.public_sentiment: Coalition includes Illinois Environmental Council, Sierra Club Illinois, Alliance for the Great Lakes, Citizens Utility Board, and IBEW Local 134. Strong opposition from Data Center Coalition, Illinois Manufacturers' Association, and the Greater Chicago Cluster of municipalities currently bound by NDAs (Elk Grove Village, Itasca, Mt. Prospect). State Senator Villivalam represents the Lincolnwood data center cluster.

general_principles.note: Public reporting of annual water intake and discharge to IL DNR.
Explicitly bans municipal NDAs covering DC energy/water consumption.
DCs must pay full cost of their energy infrastructure.
Requires community benefit agreements replacing NDAs.

timeline.milestone: Committee hearing with Alliance for the Great Lakes testimony

bills.title: Data Center Water Withdrawal Pre-Construction Notification
bills.sponsor: Rep. Joe Webster (D-150, Montgomery County)
bills.summary: Requires data centers planning to use more than 100,000 gallons of water per day over any 30-day period to notify the PA Department of Environmental Protection before commencing construction. Authorizes DEP review of proposed withdrawals against watershed capacity.
bills.status_detail: Passed PA House (~116-84) in May 2026 as part of a multi-bill data center package; stalled in the Republican-controlled Senate.

recent_news.title: The data center regulation bills on the table in PA
recent_news.takeaway: Multi-bill data center package cleared the PA House with bipartisan votes but is blocked by Senate Republican leadership.

recent_news.title: Lawmakers advance bill to give state additional oversight of new data center water use
recent_news.takeaway: Webster's bill creates the first formal PA DEP review trigger for high-volume DC water withdrawals.

bills.public_sentiment: Supported by Conservation Voters of PA, PennEnvironment, Susquehanna Riverkeeper, and Delaware Riverkeeper Network. Industrial opposition from the Data Center Coalition and PA Chamber of Business. Local activists in Cumberland County (Middlesex Township) and Lancaster County, where Amazon and other proposals are advancing, formed the regional base for the bill.

general_principles.note: Pre-construction water-use notification to state DEP.
Triggers DEP review of withdrawals above 100,000 gpd.
Watershed capacity review required before construction starts.

bills.title: Annual Data Center Energy and Water Reporting
bills.sponsor: Rep. Kyle Mullins (D-112, Lackawanna County)
bills.summary: Establishes annual energy and water reporting requirements for data centers in PA. Requires PA DEP and PUC to jointly issue annual reports on the cumulative impacts of data center energy and water use across the Commonwealth.
bills.status_detail: Passed PA House (~133-68) in May 2026 with stronger bipartisan support than companion HB 2246; stalled in PA Senate.

recent_news.title: PA House passes two bills strengthening transparency requirements, community protections related to data centers
recent_news.takeaway: HB 2150 attracted Republican crossover votes; framed as good-government transparency.

bills.public_sentiment: Broad transparency-focused coalition: PennEnvironment, PennFuture, Citizens for Pennsylvania's Future, and the PA AFL-CIO supported. PA Chamber of Business and Data Center Coalition opposed citing competitive harm but lost on the floor. Lackawanna County (Mullins' district) has multiple data center proposals advancing.

general_principles.note: Annual joint PA DEP/PUC report on aggregate DC impacts.
Per-facility annual energy and water reports.

bills.title: Ratepayer and Resource Protection Act
bills.sponsor: Rep. Lindsey Prather (D-115, Buncombe County)
bills.summary: Mandates that data centers publicly report electricity consumption, peak demand, water consumption, cooling systems, and emissions-free generation. Facilities using over 1 billion liters of water per year or peak demand >40 MW must source at least 25% of power from non-emitting generation. Repeals state sales/use tax exemption for DC construction and server replacement.
bills.status_detail: Filed April 27, 2026; referred to NC House Energy and Public Utilities Committee. Bill number to be re-verified against NC General Assembly bill lookup before citation.

recent_news.title: NC House Democrats propose data center legislation
recent_news.takeaway: First comprehensive Democratic data center proposal in NC; combines mandatory clean power with full disclosure.

recent_news.title: NC bills target data center boom, seeking tax changes, consumer protections
recent_news.takeaway: Rep. Prather's bill paired with a parallel Republican proposal; both await committee action.

bills.public_sentiment: Supported by NC Conservation Network, Southern Environmental Law Center, NC Justice Center, and AARP NC (rate concerns). Opposed by NC Chamber, NC TECH Association, and Duke Energy citing the renewable threshold as overly aggressive. The 25% clean-power floor is among the most aggressive renewable mandates in any current Southern-state data center bill.

general_principles.note: Public reporting of consumption, peak demand, and cooling systems.
25% non-emitting power requirement for largest facilities.
Repeals state sales/use tax exemption for DC equipment.

timeline.milestone: Referred to Energy and Public Utilities Committee

bills.title: Data Center Contract Review by Public Service Commission
bills.sponsor: Sen. Lance Bell (R-11, Pell City)
bills.summary: Directs the Alabama Public Service Commission to review utility contracts with large-scale data centers (≥150 MW) to ensure they provide for full recovery of incremental service costs and demonstrate 'positive benefits' for ratepayers statewide. Requires PSC findings before contracts take effect.
bills.status_detail: Passed Alabama Senate March 13, 2026; approved by Alabama House committee April 2026. Bill number to be re-verified against Alabama legislature lookup before citation.

recent_news.title: As the Alabama Legislature Adjourns, Environmentalists See a Silver Lining
recent_news.takeaway: Despite session ending with limited environmental wins, AL SB 270 represented bipartisan progress on ratepayer protection.

recent_news.title: Alabama Senate passes bill to rein in data center tax incentives
recent_news.takeaway: Sen. Bell's bill cleared Senate with bipartisan vote citing Google Bessemer and proposed DC build-out concerns.

bills.public_sentiment: Sen. Bell (R) leveraged anti-corporate-welfare framing to bring together rural Republicans and Black Caucus Democrats representing Bessemer/Jefferson County. Opposition from Alabama Power and Business Council of Alabama. Environmental groups (Alabama Rivers Alliance, GASP) supported but pushed unsuccessfully for water provisions.

general_principles.note: Requires DCs to bear full incremental service costs.
PSC pre-approval of utility-DC contracts.
Requires 'positive benefit' finding for ratepayers.

bills.title: Statewide Data Center Customer Minimum-Take Tariff
bills.sponsor: Rep. David Thomas (R-65, Jefferson) and Rep. Tristan Rader (D-13, Lakewood)
bills.summary: Codifies the PUCO-approved AEP Ohio data center tariff statewide. Requires new DC customers ≥25 MW to commit to paying for a minimum of 85% of subscribed electricity usage for up to 12 years, regardless of actual consumption. Bars utilities from recovering DC-driven costs by shifting them to other classes of customers.
bills.status_detail: Introduced February 25, 2026; referred to Ohio House Energy Committee. Bill number to be re-verified before citation.

recent_news.title: Ohio House bill would extend data center tariff to rest of state
recent_news.takeaway: Bill builds on PUCO's July 2025 approval of AEP's contested 85%-take-or-pay structure.

bills.public_sentiment: Backed by Ohio Consumers' Counsel, AARP Ohio, and the Citizens Utility Board of Ohio. The Ohio Manufacturers' Association supports the cost-allocation principle. Data Center Coalition opposes, calling the 85% minimum 'punitive.' Tristan Rader (D-Lakewood) brings progressive environmental constituency; David Thomas (R-Jefferson) brings rural ratepayer concerns. Connects to the broader Save Ohio Parks petition to ban DCs.

general_principles.note: 85% minimum-take ensures DCs cover utility's stranded capacity investment.
Prohibits cost-shifting to residential and small commercial customers.
Codifies AEP/PUCO model statewide.

timeline.milestone: PUCO approves AEP Ohio data center tariff (approximate)

bills.title: Artificial Intelligence Data Center Moratorium Act
bills.sponsor: Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT); companion in House by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY-14)
bills.summary: Imposes a federal moratorium on construction of new AI data centers until safeguards are enacted ensuring the facilities do not increase utility bills, exacerbate climate impacts, deny community veto authority, or undermine labor standards. Also bans export of US AI computing infrastructure to countries without environmental, labor, and safety safeguards.
bills.status_detail: Introduced March 25, 2026; read twice and referred to Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

recent_news.title: Sanders, Ocasio-Cortez Announce AI Data Center Moratorium Act
recent_news.takeaway: Most aggressive federal proposal; ties lifting the moratorium to community veto authority and union jobs.

recent_news.title: State Data Center Laws vs. Federal AI Push: 2026 Tracker
recent_news.takeaway: S 4214 named as the headline federal counterweight to the Trump permit-acceleration order.

bills.public_sentiment: Endorsed by AFL-CIO, Sierra Club, Sunrise Movement, Public Citizen, and the AI Now Institute. Sharply opposed by the Trump White House, Data Center Coalition, US Chamber of Commerce, and bipartisan critics who consider it an AI race-against-China risk. Symbolic value high; legislative path unlikely in the Republican Senate.

general_principles.note: Hard pause on new AI DCs pending federal safeguard legislation.
Sets a federal floor preempting state-by-state variation.
Conditions lifting moratorium on labor and community standards.

bills.title: Power for the People Act of 2026
bills.sponsor: Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD); cosponsors Durbin (D-IL), Blumenthal (D-CT), Booker (D-NJ), Duckworth (D-IL), Smith (D-MN), Welch (D-VT), Alsobrooks (D-MD)
bills.summary: Directs FERC to require grid operators to establish 'data center load queues' allowing utilities to prioritize or delay DC interconnections based on grid reliability and affordability. Encourages every state with at least one DC to establish DC-specific rate classes ensuring DC owners bear the full cost of generation, transmission, and distribution upgrades they trigger.
bills.status_detail: Introduced January 15, 2026; referred to Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.

recent_news.title: Van Hollen Leads New Bill to Ensure Americans Aren't Footing the Bill for Big Data Centers
recent_news.takeaway: Eight-cosponsor Democratic bill positioning FERC as the central federal lever for DC cost allocation.

recent_news.title: LIUNA endorses Van Hollen Power for the People Act
recent_news.takeaway: Building trades labor endorsement bolsters bill's Democratic-coalition support.

bills.public_sentiment: Supported by AARP, NRDC, Sierra Club, LIUNA, and consumer rate advocates including the Energy and Policy Institute. Skeptical: PJM Interconnection, the Electric Power Supply Association, and the Data Center Coalition. Cosponsorship spans Northeast and Midwest senators whose states bear early DC cost pressure.

general_principles.note: DCs pay full cost of grid expansion they cause.
FERC required to establish DC load queue framework.
Grid operators authorized to prioritize or delay DC interconnections.

timeline.milestone: Referred to Senate Energy & Natural Resources Committee

bills.title: Stopping Hikes In Electricity from Large Load Demands (SHIELD) Act
bills.sponsor: Rep. Mike Levin (D-CA-49); Rep. Kathy Castor (D-FL-14) co-lead
bills.summary: Updates federal utility cost-allocation policy under PURPA so that large electricity users like data centers bear the costs of grid infrastructure they require, while incentivizing zero-emission electricity sourcing. Aims to prevent cost-shifting onto residential and small commercial ratepayers.
bills.status_detail: Introduced February 2026; referred to House Energy and Commerce Committee. Bill number to be re-verified against Congress.gov before citation.

recent_news.title: Rep. Mike Levin Introduces SHIELD Act to Stop Data Centers from Driving Up Electricity Prices
recent_news.takeaway: House Democratic companion track to Van Hollen Senate bill; emphasizes zero-emission sourcing.

bills.public_sentiment: Supported by NRDC, Earthjustice, League of Conservation Voters, and California consumer advocacy groups. The Data Center Coalition and US Chamber of Commerce oppose. Levin's district covers North County San Diego where Microsoft and Apple have facilities; Castor's covers Tampa with significant data-center build-out.

general_principles.note: Federal PURPA update directing utilities to shield ratepayers from DC infrastructure costs.
Standardizes large-load cost recovery rules across states.
Incentivizes zero-emission electricity for large loads.

timeline.milestone: Introduced by Reps. Levin and Castor

bills.title: AI Data Center Site Selection Transparency Act of 2026
bills.sponsor: Rep. LaMonica McIver (D-NJ-10); cosponsors Rep. Valerie Foushee (D-NC-4), Rep. Andre Carson (D-IN-7)
bills.summary: Requires AI data center developers to publicly disclose proposed sites at least 180 days before any definitive development step. Mandates community engagement, multilingual outreach, and disclosure of projected electricity use, water consumption, cooling demands, and environmental impacts. Restricts NDAs and treats violations as unfair or deceptive practices under the FTC Act.
bills.status_detail: Introduced May 2026; referred to House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

recent_news.title: McIver Introduces Bill to Stop Surprise AI Data Center Development
recent_news.takeaway: First federal bill imposing pre-construction public disclosure with FTC enforcement teeth.

bills.public_sentiment: Backed by NAACP, LULAC, Public Citizen, Sierra Club, and the National Association of Counties. Industry opposition from Data Center Coalition, NetChoice, and TechNet. McIver represents Newark, NJ where industrial-zone DC proposals are advancing; Foushee covers the North Carolina Triangle region with major Microsoft/Google build-outs.

general_principles.note: 180-day public pre-disclosure window before any definitive development step.
Public disclosure of energy, water, cooling, and environmental impact projections.
Restricts NDAs covering DC siting decisions.
Violations treated as unfair/deceptive practices under FTC Act.

timeline.milestone: Referred to House Energy and Commerce Committee

bills.title: Draft NPDES General Permit for Discharges from Data Center Facilities
bills.sponsor: Ohio EPA Division of Surface Water (agency rulemaking)
bills.summary: First-of-its-kind NPDES general permit covering data center wastewater and stormwater discharges to waters of the state. Eligible facilities could obtain coverage for non-contact cooling water, cooling tower blowdown, boiler blowdown, air compressor condensate, and industrial stormwater via Notice of Intent (NOI) rather than individual NPDES permits. Sets monitoring parameters: temperature, pH, TSS, oil and grease, phosphorus, residual chlorine/oxidants.
bills.status_detail: Regulatory rulemaking, not a bill. Draft public-noticed October 31, 2025; public hearing December 17, 2025; comment period closed January 16, 2026. Final permit pending Ohio EPA action; five-year permit term once issued.

recent_news.title: Ohio EPA reviewing draft permit to authorize limited increase in data center wastewater discharge
recent_news.takeaway: Ohio EPA reviewing comments; opposition from environmental groups citing inadequate cumulative-impact analysis.

recent_news.title: Tell Ohio EPA: New data center wastewater permit puts our waters at risk
recent_news.takeaway: Alliance and Save Ohio Parks led environmental opposition arguing general permitting shortcuts individual review.

bills.public_sentiment: Industry (Data Center Coalition, Ohio Chamber, Columbus Partnership) strongly supports the general permit as streamlining build-out. Environmental opposition (Alliance for the Great Lakes, Sierra Club Ohio, Ohio Environmental Council, Save Ohio Parks) argues general permitting circumvents site-specific cumulative-impact analysis required under the Clean Water Act. Ohio EPA is under pressure from both the Trump White House permit-acceleration order and Save Ohio Parks ballot initiative gathering signatures by July 1, 2026.

general_principles.note: Replaces individual NPDES permits with general-permit NOI process.
Standardizes monitoring parameters for DC wastewater.
Monitoring data publicly available through DMR submissions.

monitor.note: Draft general permit still not finalized; finalization makes data centers direct DMR filers.

bills.title: Zoning Ordinance Amendment Eliminating By-Right Data Center Development
bills.sponsor: Loudoun County Board of Supervisors (Chair Phyllis Randall, D-At-Large lead)
bills.summary: Comprehensive zoning ordinance amendment removing by-right (administrative) approval pathway for data centers in Loudoun County. Now requires Special Exception (SPEX) approval with stringent legislative review and public hearings before Planning Commission and Board of Supervisors. Phase 2 (expected late 2026) will further tighten compatibility, water, and noise standards.
bills.status_detail: ZOAM/CPAM adopted March 18, 2025. Phase 2 draft to Board May 2026; Planning Commission hearings July 2026; full Board action expected December 2026.

recent_news.title: Loudoun County Board approves Data Center Standards and Locations Phase 2 Project Plan
recent_news.takeaway: Phase 2 will address compatibility, noise, water use, and visual impact standards via SPEX process.

recent_news.title: Loudoun County, Virginia, Eliminates By-Right Data Center Development
recent_news.takeaway: First major hyperscale-cluster county to eliminate by-right DC approvals; sets template for other Northern Virginia jurisdictions.

bills.public_sentiment: Driven by grassroots opposition led by Piedmont Environmental Council, Coalition to Protect Prince William County, Loudoun Sierra Club, and residents of Aldie, Bluemont, and rural-western Loudoun. The Data Center Coalition vigorously opposed; the bipartisan Board nonetheless voted unanimously after extensive public comment. State enabling authority is robust under Virginia's general zoning powers; a hard moratorium would require legislative authorization.

general_principles.note: Mandatory legislative review with public hearings for every new DC.
Eliminates administrative approval pathway.
Phase 2 will standardize compatibility, noise, water use standards.

timeline.milestone: ZOAM/CPAM adopted by Board of Supervisors

bills.title: Data Centers — Limitations on Consumptive Use of Water for Cooling
bills.sponsor: House Ways and Means Committee (Rep. Britt Raybould, R-Rexburg, a leading proponent)
bills.summary: Requires data centers built after July 1, 2026 to design cooling systems for non-consumptive water use or to draw from a municipal/water-district system, and requires the Department of Water Resources director to issue findings when evaluating new water appropriations or transfers for data centers. Aimed at preserving groundwater for agriculture in Idaho's high desert.
bills.status_detail: Signed by Gov. Little April 2, 2026 (Session Law Ch. 291); effective July 1, 2026. Verified on legislature.idaho.gov.

recent_news.title: Idaho advances bill on data center water consumption
recent_news.takeaway: Bill passed the House 58-10 and won a do-pass from Senate Resources & Environment, framed as protecting agricultural water in Idaho's high desert.

bills.public_sentiment: Broad bipartisan support driven by agricultural water users worried about aquifer depletion; passed both chambers by lopsided margins (58-10 House, 32-1 Senate) with little organized industry opposition since municipal-supplied data centers remain permitted.

general_principles.note: Mandates non-consumptive cooling design for new data centers not on municipal systems, effectively requiring closed-loop or equivalent designs.
Requires IDWR director findings before approving new water appropriations or transfers for data centers.
Explicitly preserves consumptive water rights for agriculture and existing industry over new data center demand.

timeline.detail: Session Law Chapter 291, effective July 1, 2026

bills.title: Data Center Bill of Rights for Citizens
bills.sponsor: Sen. Pres. Pro Tempore Chris Karr (R-Sioux Falls) & House Speaker Jon Hansen (R-Dell Rapids)
bills.summary: Data centers with peak electrical demand of 10 MW or greater must cover the electrical-infrastructure costs they cause (including stranded costs if they leave) and must coordinate with water service providers so their water use stays within locally approved supply; the state may not preempt local ordinances regulating data centers.
bills.status_detail: Signed by Gov. Larry Rhoden March 24, 2026; applies to data centers >=10 MW peak demand. The only data-center bill to pass the 2026 session (moratorium and tax-incentive bills failed); the Public Utilities Commission may charge regulatory-review costs to operators.

recent_news.title: Data center restrictions signed into South Dakota law after push for incentives failed
recent_news.takeaway: Gov. Rhoden signed SB 135 after lawmakers rejected both a moratorium and tax incentives; the law makes large data centers pay their own infrastructure costs and protects local water supply.

recent_news.title: Data center regulation bill passes South Dakota House
recent_news.takeaway: House passed an amended SB 135 60-7, advancing the 10-MW threshold and the water-compatibility requirement to the governor.

recent_news.title: Bill to regulate data centers heads to governor's desk
recent_news.takeaway: Sponsors called it a 'Data Center Bill of Rights' protecting ratepayers and local water providers from being overburdened by large facilities.

bills.public_sentiment: Sponsored by South Dakota's top legislative leaders (Senate President Pro Tempore Chris Karr and House Speaker Jon Hansen) and framed as ratepayer/water protection, it passed with wide margins after the Legislature rejected both a data-center moratorium and tax incentives. Tribal advocates (reported by Buffalo's Fire) raised concerns about the law's broader data-center framework, while industry resisted the cost-causation and local-control provisions.

general_principles.note: Requires data centers >=10 MW to pay the electrical-infrastructure costs they cause, including if they exit.
Data centers must coordinate with water service providers so their use stays within locally approved supply.
Bars the state from preempting local ordinances that limit or regulate data centers.

timeline.detail: House Do Pass Amended, 60-7.
Signed by Gov. Larry Rhoden.

bills.title: Data Center Water Transparency Amendments
bills.sponsor: Rep. Jill Koford (R-Ogden)
bills.summary: Large data centers (redefined as 10,000+ sq ft, down from 50,000) must notify water providers of their projected water demand and report their actual water consumption to the state. A committee substitute made the water data more publicly transparent after criticism that the original version would have shielded individual facilities' use from public records.
bills.status_detail: Signed by Gov. Spencer Cox March 23, 2026 (among 87 bills signed that session); lowers the 'large data center' threshold to 10,000 sq ft. Default effective date ~60 days after the 2026 session adjourned (early May 2026).

recent_news.title: New bill forces Utah data centers to disclose water use estimates
recent_news.takeaway: Great Salt Lake Waterkeeper's Zach Frankel warned two data centers can use as much water as a city of 100,000; the law makes new facilities disclose projected and actual use.

recent_news.title: How Utah's 2026 legislative session reshaped water policy
recent_news.takeaway: HB 76 is highlighted among the session's data-center water measures, requiring large facilities to notify providers and report consumption.

bills.public_sentiment: Great Salt Lake Waterkeeper (Zach Frankel) hailed the final bill as a transparency victory after public pushback forced sponsor Rep. Jill Koford to substitute a version that makes water-use data more public rather than exempt from disclosure. The data-center industry called the reporting 'burdensome' and warned it could deter investment, but the bill passed and Gov. Cox signed it; weeks later Cox issued an executive order setting higher water standards for new data-center development.

general_principles.note: Makes large data centers' projected and actual water use visible to the state and, after the substitute, more public.
Requires operators to notify water providers of projected demand and report actual consumption.
Lowers the 'large data center' threshold to 10,000 sq ft so more facilities fall under the reporting regime.

timeline.detail: HB 76 by Rep. Jill Koford; substitute adopted in committee during week one after public criticism.
Cleared both chambers as the 2026 general session closed.
Signed by Gov. Spencer Cox among 87 bills.

bills.title: High-impact data center / microgrid certification rule (Dept. of Commerce)
bills.sponsor: House Energy & Public Works Committee (Dept. of Commerce legislative rule bundle)
bills.summary: Authorizes a Dept. of Commerce legislative rule setting the certification process for 'high impact' data centers and microgrid districts (implementing 2025's HB 2014) and keeps key project details confidential. A Senate amendment added only soft language directing that potential water use be 'studied' and water sources given 'mindful protections'; floor amendments to require pre-operation water-impact assessments and to limit groundwater use were rejected.
bills.status_detail: Approved by Gov. Patrick Morrisey March 27, 2026. House passed 78-16 (Feb 17); Senate passed an amended version 28-6 (~Mar 11). Implements the certified-microgrid / high-impact-data-center program from 2025 HB 2014. Water-protection amendments were defeated, leaving only non-binding 'study'/'mindful protection' language.

recent_news.title: WV House passes new data center development rules without local control, water protection provisions
recent_news.takeaway: The House passed HB 4983 78-16 after rejecting amendments that would have required water-impact assessments and limited groundwater use for data centers.

recent_news.title: WV Senate passes data center rules with new language urging developers to study potential water use
recent_news.takeaway: The Senate added only soft language directing that potential water use be studied and water sources given 'mindful protections,' stopping short of binding limits.

recent_news.title: Data center rule amended, returns to House
recent_news.takeaway: The amended rule bundle returned to the House for concurrence before heading to Gov. Morrisey.

bills.public_sentiment: WV Rivers Coalition, Conservation West Virginia, and legislators including Del. Laura Kimble criticized HB 4983 for stripping local control and rejecting binding water-use transparency and groundwater limits, leaving only a non-binding 'study' directive; advocates noted large data centers can use 3-5 million gallons/day. The Morrisey administration and Dept. of Commerce backed it as implementing the 2025 high-impact-data-center/microgrid program, and it passed both chambers comfortably.

general_principles.note: Keeps basic information about proposed high-impact data center projects shielded from public disclosure.
Sets the state certification process for high-impact data centers and microgrid districts.
Rejected amendments would have required pre-operation water-impact assessments and groundwater limits; only non-binding 'study' language survived.

timeline.detail: House passed 78-16; water-protection amendments rejected.
Senate passed an amended version 28-6.
House concurrence on the amended rule bundle.
Approved by Gov. Patrick Morrisey.

bills.title: Data Center Impact Analysis and Report
bills.sponsor: Sen. Karen Lewis Young & Sen. Stephen Ready (SB 116); HB 270 House companion
bills.summary: Commissions a state study of the environmental, energy, and economic impacts of data center development: the Dept. of the Environment assesses effects on air and water quality and Chesapeake Bay restoration, the Maryland Energy Administration assesses energy demand and infrastructure, and the University of Maryland School of Business covers economic impacts. The report is due to the Governor and General Assembly by Sept. 1, 2026.
bills.status_detail: 2025 Regular Session. Vetoed by Gov. Wes Moore (May 2025); the General Assembly overrode the veto Dec. 16, 2025, enacting it. ~$502K study; report due Sept. 1, 2026.

recent_news.title: Climate study, energy planning, data center bills become law after Moore vetoes are overridden
recent_news.takeaway: The General Assembly overrode Gov. Moore's veto of the data-center impact study, enacting the requirement that MDE and MEA quantify water, energy, and economic impacts.

recent_news.title: Maryland General Assembly overrides veto on data center impact report
recent_news.takeaway: Override coverage details the $502K study examining electricity demand, water resources, infrastructure costs, and local economies, due September 2026.

bills.public_sentiment: Environmental groups (including Nature Forward) and legislative leadership backed the study and supplied the supermajority to override Gov. Wes Moore's veto; Moore (D) had argued it was duplicative and burdensome. The data-center industry was wary of a state impact study that could inform future siting and permitting rules, while advocates framed it as a prerequisite to responsible data-center growth in Maryland.

general_principles.note: A state-commissioned study makes data centers' water, energy, and economic effects public.
Requires MDE and the Maryland Energy Administration to quantify water-quality, Bay-restoration, and energy-demand impacts.
Findings are intended to inform future data-center siting and permitting policy.

timeline.detail: Cleared both chambers in the 2025 Regular Session.
Vetoed by Gov. Wes Moore.
General Assembly overrode the veto, enacting the study.

bills.title: Data center sustainability reporting and grid protections
bills.sponsor: Rep. Beth Doglio (D-Olympia)
bills.summary: Would have required data center operators to file a sustainability report disclosing server-cooling technology and water/energy use and emissions, directed utilities to adopt a data-center cost-recovery tariff by 2027 so other ratepayers do not subsidize them, and required large loads to curtail electricity use during grid stress.
bills.status_detail: Passed House Appropriations in mid-February 2026 but died when it failed to advance before the 2026 session's cutoff (early March 2026). A Republican-backed amendment had stripped the annual operator fee and loosened clean-energy terms; the sponsor signaled reintroduction in 2027.

recent_news.title: It's lights out for WA Legislature's effort to regulate data centers
recent_news.takeaway: HB 2515 died at the session cutoff after tech-industry pressure weakened it; Rep. Doglio said she would keep working on the legislation next year.

recent_news.title: How Washington state lawmakers are trying to regulate data centers
recent_news.takeaway: The bill would have required sustainability reports on cooling technology and water/energy use plus a utility cost-recovery tariff and emergency curtailment.

recent_news.title: How WA lawmakers are trying to regulate data centers
recent_news.takeaway: Early coverage details the transparency and ratepayer-protection design before amendments weakened the bill in committee.

bills.public_sentiment: Sponsor Rep. Beth Doglio, environmental groups, and ratepayer advocates backed HB 2515 over grid-reliability and water-strain concerns. Tech companies gained ground against it (per the Daily Chronicle) and a Republican-backed amendment stripped the operator fee and loosened clean-energy requirements before the bill stalled at the cutoff; advocates argued Washington 'can't afford to wait' on data-center rules.

general_principles.note: Sustainability report on cooling technology, water/energy use, and emissions.
Utility data-center cost-recovery tariff by 2027 so other ratepayers aren't subsidizing large loads.
Mandatory curtailment of large data-center loads during grid stress.

timeline.detail: Advanced out of committee in mid-February.
Failed to advance before the 2026 session deadline.

bills.title: Data center development and electricity reporting
bills.sponsor: Sen. J.D. Ford (D) & Sen. Spencer Deery (R)
bills.summary: Would have created an Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission working group to forecast data-center electricity demand (report by Oct. 31, 2026), required operators to file quarterly electricity-use reports the IURC publishes online, and required local governments to obtain projected power and water-use disclosures plus a site assessment before issuing data-center permits.
bills.status_detail: Died in the 2026 session - never granted a hearing in the Senate Utilities Committee. Bipartisan sponsorship (Ford D / Deery R).

recent_news.title: That 1% incentive to encourage data center approvals? Final deal watered it down
recent_news.takeaway: Indiana's 2026 session ended with little binding data-center oversight; transparency bills like SB 79 stalled while a weakened local-incentive deal advanced.

recent_news.title: State Data Center Legislation in 2026 Tackles Energy and Tax Issues
recent_news.takeaway: Indiana was among states weighing data-center electricity-reporting and demand-forecasting bills, with SB 79 pairing IURC reporting with local power/water disclosure.

bills.public_sentiment: The Citizens Action Coalition and consumer/environmental advocates backed SB 79 for ratepayer protection and transparency, but it never received a Senate Utilities Committee hearing in a session where Indiana lawmakers largely deferred to utilities and a watered-down tax-incentive deal. Its bipartisan sponsorship (Sens. J.D. Ford and Spencer Deery) underscored cross-party interest in disclosure even as the bill died.

general_principles.note: Quarterly operator electricity-use reports published online, plus local projected power and water-use disclosure before permitting.
IURC working group to estimate future data-center electricity demand and report by Oct. 31, 2026.
Requires a site assessment and disclosures before a county/municipality issues a data-center permit.

timeline.detail: Filed for the 2026 session by Sens. Ford and Deery.
Never granted a hearing in the Senate Utilities Committee before session end.

bills.title: Responsible Data Center Development Act (one-year moratorium)
bills.sponsor: Sen. Kristen Gonzalez (D-59th); Assembly companion A11560
bills.summary: Imposes a one-year statewide moratorium on permits for hyperscale data centers (peak load over 20 MW), requires environmental impact reporting on water consumption, discharge, and local water-system impacts, mandates separate water and electricity rate classes for large data centers, and pushes measures such as closed-loop cooling to prevent wastewater-infrastructure strain.
bills.status_detail: Passed both chambers June 2026 — the first statewide data-center moratorium bill to clear a legislature. Gov. Hochul neither signed nor vetoed it; on 2026-07-14 she superseded it with Executive Order 62, which imposes a one-year DEC permit moratorium at a 50 MW threshold rather than the bill's 20 MW. Track NY EO 62 for the operative instrument; an eventual veto of this bill is the expected outcome.

recent_news.title: New York State Gets One Step Closer to a Data Center Moratorium
recent_news.takeaway: The legislature passed the first-in-nation statewide hyperscale data center moratorium in the session's final hours.

recent_news.title: NY Gov. Hochul Must Sign One-Year AI Data Center Moratorium Passed by Legislature
recent_news.takeaway: Environmental groups are pressuring Hochul to sign, citing water and energy strain from hyperscale facilities.

bills.public_sentiment: Strong support from environmental groups (Earthjustice, Food & Water Watch), labor, and consumer advocates; opposed by tech and business groups warning it will push AI investment to other states. Gov. Hochul's position is uncertain given her economic-development agenda.

general_principles.note: One-year statewide pause on permits for data centers over 20 MW.
Requires environmental impact reporting on water consumption, discharge, and local water-system effects.
Creates separate rate classes so large data centers bear their full water and electric infrastructure costs.
Directs mitigation measures, potentially including closed-loop cooling, to prevent water pollution and wastewater strain.

timeline.detail: Late-session print of the Responsible Data Center Development Act

timeline.milestone: Passed Assembly via substitution of A11560 (102-39)

monitor.note: Never signed or vetoed — superseded by EO 62. Watch for an eventual veto.

bills.title: Higher Bar for Data Center Development (Executive Order)
bills.sponsor: Gov. Spencer Cox
bills.summary: Directs all state agencies to weigh water use (specifically Great Salt Lake impacts), air quality, wildlife, utility ratepayer costs, and public transparency alongside economic growth when reviewing data center projects. Creates formal Data Center Framework for state agency review.
bills.status_detail: Signed May 29, 2026 by Governor Spencer Cox; effective immediately. Supplements enacted HB 76 water transparency law. Triggered by public backlash over Stratos Data Center proposal in Box Elder County.

recent_news.title: Gov. Cox executive order on data centers effective immediately
recent_news.takeaway: Directs agencies to balance water/environment against economic development; Great Salt Lake impact specifically named.

bills.public_sentiment: Strong local community support around Great Salt Lake protection. Business community cautiously supportive.

general_principles.note: Directs state agencies to establish water-use reporting requirements for large data center projects before permitting.
EO instructs UDNR to evaluate water-cost attribution so data center developers bear marginal costs of supply expansion.

timeline.detail: Gov. Spencer Cox signed EO 2026-03, effective immediately

bills.title: Water Resources: Data Centers — Water Use Disclosure
bills.sponsor: Assemblymember Diane Papan
bills.summary: Requires data center operators to disclose projected water use, source, and volumes to their water supplier before obtaining a business license; upon renewal, requires reporting of actual annual water consumption. Directs DWR and CEC to develop water efficiency best practices by Jan 1, 2029. Successor to vetoed CA AB 93 (2025).
bills.status_detail: Passed Assembly Water, Parks, and Wildlife Committee April 2026; advancing through Assembly/Senate committees as of June 2026. Paired with SB 887 (Padilla). Preceded by CA AB 93 (same author, vetoed by Newsom Oct 2025).

recent_news.title: California data centers face water transparency push after Newsom veto
recent_news.takeaway: AB 2619 is the successor to vetoed AB 93; similar industry opposition expected but Papan pressing again.

bills.public_sentiment: Environmental groups, water agencies, and local governments supportive. Tech industry opposing mandatory disclosure provisions; similar objections led to Newsom's 2025 AB 93 veto.

general_principles.note: Requires data centers ≥10,000 sq ft to publicly report projected and actual water consumption annually.
Successor to vetoed AB 93 with narrowed scope; reporting threshold lowered to match water-district metering capabilities.

timeline.detail: Re-introduced by Asm. Papan for 2025-26 session; successor to vetoed AB 93

timeline.milestone: Passed Assembly Water, Parks, and Wildlife Committee

bills.title: Data Center CEQA Environmental Review
bills.sponsor: Sen. Steve Padilla
bills.summary: Prohibits categorical CEQA exemptions for data center projects; creates expedited judicial review pathway for data centers meeting clean energy and water efficiency standards under the Environmental Leadership Development Project program. Companion to AB 2619.
bills.status_detail: Passed Senate 29-9; heard in Assembly Natural Resources Committee June 22, 2026. Companion to AB 2619.

recent_news.title: SB 887 heard in Assembly Natural Resources Committee
recent_news.takeaway: Paired with AB 2619 as twin data center environmental accountability measures advancing through CA legislature.

bills.public_sentiment: Environmental coalition strongly supportive. Tech industry opposes CEQA de-exemption; developers argue ELDP pathway offsets the change.

general_principles.note: Subjects new data center construction to CEQA review, including a mandatory water-supply assessment.
Companion to AB 2619: CEQA findings must include projected water demand over 30-year facility life.

bills.title: POWER Act — Data Center Energy and Water Requirements
bills.sponsor: Sen. Ram Villivalam
bills.summary: Would have required data centers to source renewable energy, submit quarterly water use reports, and submit water management plans to the IL Water Survey. Included community benefits agreements and ratepayer protection provisions.
bills.status_detail: Failed — did not pass before Illinois General Assembly session ended May 31, 2026. Gov. Pritzker responded by pausing new Data Center Investment Program tax incentive agreements starting July 1, 2026. Expected to return in November 2026 veto session.

recent_news.title: Illinois POWER Act fails; Pritzker pauses data center tax incentives
recent_news.takeaway: Bill failed but Pritzker incentive pause signals executive pressure continues; expected in fall veto session.

bills.public_sentiment: Strong support from environmental advocates, labor, and community groups. Opposed by data center industry and utility companies citing compliance burden.

general_principles.note: Requires disclosure of water and power demand projections as condition for tax incentive eligibility.
Ratepayer-protection provisions: data center grid costs cannot be socialized to residential customers.

timeline.milestone: Pritzker pauses new Data Center Investment Program incentive agreements
timeline.detail: Executive action in response to POWER Act failure

bills.title: Data Center Development Moratorium
bills.sponsor: Sen. Jim Runestad (R); Reps. Wortz, Wegela (D), Fox (R) [HB 5594-5596]
bills.summary: Bipartisan package that would halt data center development until April 1, 2027, pending development of comprehensive water, energy, and environmental standards.
bills.status_detail: Pending in Senate Government Operations Committee as of June 2026. Leadership prefers regulation over prohibition; no hearing scheduled. Renewed bipartisan public push at Capitol event June 23-24, 2026.

recent_news.title: Michigan lawmakers, residents renew push for statewide data center moratorium
recent_news.takeaway: Bipartisan event June 23 at Capitol renewed momentum; Senate leadership prefers targeted regulation over moratorium.

bills.public_sentiment: Bipartisan resident, farmer, and environmental organization support. Data center industry and economic development groups strongly opposing.

general_principles.note: Imposes a moratorium on new data center construction permits until state water-capacity analysis is complete.
Paired bills require Great Lakes Compact review for any facility drawing >100,000 GPD from surface or groundwater.

timeline.milestone: Bipartisan Capitol event renews push for moratorium
timeline.detail: No hearing scheduled; Senate leadership prefers targeted regulation

bills.title: Data Center Responsibility Act — Closed-Loop Cooling Mandate
bills.sponsor: SC House (bipartisan)
bills.summary: Requires data centers to use closed-loop cooling systems resulting in zero net water withdrawal and net zero wastewater discharge; prohibits groundwater extraction or municipal water use for cooling.
bills.status_detail: Introduced January 2026; in House committee. SC General Assembly adjourned May 2026; likely carried over to 2027 session.

recent_news.title: State data center water usage legislation gains momentum
recent_news.takeaway: SC leads with most aggressive zero-withdrawal mandate among 2026 state bills.

bills.public_sentiment: Strong environmental advocate support, particularly coastal plain communities. Data center industry strongly opposed as technically infeasible for most existing cooling designs.

general_principles.note: Mandates closed-loop (zero-discharge) cooling for new data centers over 10 MW to eliminate consumptive evaporative water loss.

timeline.milestone: SC General Assembly adjourned; bill carried over to 2027

bills.title: Cloud Computing Cluster Infrastructure Grant Fund — Treated Wastewater Cooling Condition
bills.sponsor: Patron not confirmed — re-verify on Virginia LIS
bills.summary: Conditions eligibility for Cloud Computing Cluster Infrastructure Grant Fund awards on the data center using treated (reclaimed) wastewater rather than potable water in its cooling systems — an incentive-based approach rather than a cooling-technology mandate.
bills.status_detail: Did not clear the Senate before the 2026 crossover deadline; reported as carried over for consideration when the legislature reconvenes in 2027. Could not load lis.virginia.gov bill page (JS-only) — re-verify bill status, patron, and continuation on Virginia LIS.

recent_news.title: State Data Center Water Usage Legislation Gains Momentum
recent_news.takeaway: MultiState highlights SB 417 as Virginia's incentive-based alternative to closed-loop mandates, tying grant money to reclaimed-water cooling.

recent_news.title: What's in the water? What we know and don't know about data center water discharge in Virginia
recent_news.takeaway: Continuing scrutiny of Virginia data center water use keeps pressure on incentive bills like SB 417 ahead of the 2027 session.

bills.public_sentiment: Conservation groups view it as a modest but workable carrot; industry prefers it to mandates like SC H 4583 or KS SB 400 since Amazon and others are already expanding recycled-water cooling. Skeptics note it only binds grant recipients, not all operators.

general_principles.note: Attaches environmental strings to state grant subsidies rather than handing them out unconditionally.
Shifts cooling demand from potable supplies to treated wastewater.
Uses incentives, not mandates, to steer operators toward reclaimed-water cooling.

timeline.detail: Exact introduction date to re-verify on LIS
Date approximate — crossover deadline of 2026 session

timeline.milestone: Expected reconsideration when legislature reconvenes in 2027

bills.bill_id: US S. — Data Center Water and Energy Transparency Act (Durbin; number TBD)
bills.title: Data Center Water and Energy Transparency Act
bills.sponsor: Sen. Dick Durbin (D-IL)
bills.summary: Would require data-center operators to report actual energy and water consumption (plus five-year pre-construction estimates) to their states; states would aggregate/anonymize data for EPA, DOE, and USDA, who would issue joint regional reports and could fine non-compliance.
bills.status_detail: Introduced ~2026-03-25 per Senator's press release. Canonical S. bill number not confirmed against Congress.gov; do not confuse with S. 4214 (AI Data Center Moratorium Act, introduced the same day).

recent_news.title: Data center boom raises water, power questions
recent_news.takeaway: Day-after coverage notes the bill responds to ~4,000 active and ~3,000 planned U.S. data centers and a 100-MW facility's water use roughly equaling 2,600 households.

recent_news.title: As Utility Costs Rise, Durbin Introduces New Legislation To Bring Transparency To Energy & Water Consumption By Data Centers
recent_news.takeaway: Original release: 5-year pre-construction projections, state-level reporting, EPA/DOE/USDA aggregated regional reports, and per-day fines for noncompliance.

bills.public_sentiment: Coverage is thin and no formal endorsements have been published in available reporting. The bill aligns with positions taken by Sierra Club Illinois, the Illinois Clean Jobs Coalition, and environmental advocates pushing parallel state-level transparency (Illinois POWER Act). No direct Data Center Coalition or NetChoice response to this specific federal bill has surfaced, though DCC has opposed similar prescriptive transparency provisions in Illinois state legislation. Durbin introduced it solo with no Senate cosponsors at launch.

general_principles.note: Mandates actual + 5-year projected energy and water consumption disclosure for new and existing facilities.
Requires pre-construction estimates so local governments can evaluate before approving facilities.
States aggregate and anonymize data for EPA, DOE, and USDA joint regional reports.
Frames disclosure as a response to data center demand driving up consumer utility costs.

timeline.detail: Sen. Dick Durbin (D-IL) introduced solo; Senate bill number not yet confirmed in public Congress.gov listings as of late May 2026.

monitor.note: Bill number still unassigned in the record; watch for introduction.

bills.title: Large-Load Data Centers
bills.sponsor: Sen. Cathy Kipp (D-Fort Collins); Rep. Kyle Brown (D)
bills.summary: Would have required operators of new large-load data centers to comply with operational water management requirements and to report annual electricity and water consumption to the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (first reports due June 30, 2028). Killed in committee at the sponsor's request.
bills.status_detail: Postponed indefinitely 9-0 by Senate Transportation & Energy Committee on May 11, 2026, four days after companion HB26-1030 died. Verified on leg.colorado.gov.

recent_news.title: Both Colorado data center bills rejected in final days of 2026 legislative session
recent_news.takeaway: Both SB26-102 and companion HB26-1030 died amid heavy industry lobbying, leaving Colorado with no statewide data center water rules.

recent_news.title: Colorado killed its only data center water bills. Cities are filling the gap themselves.
recent_news.takeaway: With the state bills dead, Denver, Jefferson County, and Longmont began writing their own data center water rules.

bills.public_sentiment: Environmental and ratepayer groups backed the disclosure mandates; 238 lobbyists for 221 clients registered on the two bills, with data center and utility interests arguing the mandates were too restrictive for 24/7 facilities and would deter investment. Its death triggered local-government backlash and municipal moratoriums.

general_principles.note: Required annual water and electricity consumption reporting to state health officials.
Imposed operational water-management requirements on large-load data centers.
Would have made data center resource use visible to regulators and the public for the first time in Colorado.

timeline.milestone: Introduced in Senate; assigned to Transportation & Energy Committee
Committee hearing; amendments failed, bill laid over

bills.title: Certain Requirements Related to Data Centers (water recycling and reporting)
bills.sponsor: Reps. Zimmerman, Wittke et al. (R); Senate cosponsors Quinn, Feyen et al.
bills.summary: Would have required data centers to recycle the water used to cool computer equipment, report water usage to the Wisconsin DNR, and meet utility-rate requirements ensuring facilities, not residential ratepayers, pay for their energy and water infrastructure demands.
bills.status_detail: Passed Assembly 53-44 on Jan 20, 2026; Senate committee recommended concurrence March 13, 2026 but the Senate never passed it before the session ended — died at adjournment. Verified history on docs.legis.wisconsin.gov; re-verify exact final Senate disposition (failure-to-concur date).

recent_news.title: Wisconsin Assembly advances bill to regulate data centers
recent_news.takeaway: GOP-led AB 840 passed the Assembly with water-recycling and DNR water-reporting mandates after Democratic amendments failed.

recent_news.title: Wisconsin's Data Center Reckoning: Four Bills, No Resolution, and a Policy Vacuum
recent_news.takeaway: None of Wisconsin's four data center bills became law, leaving a regulatory vacuum despite bipartisan concern.

bills.public_sentiment: Republican authors framed it as protecting ratepayers and water resources; Democrats wanted stronger renewable-energy and labor provisions and mostly voted no, while conservation groups like River Alliance of Wisconsin pushed for tougher water safeguards. Industry was wary of the recycling mandate.

general_principles.note: Required data centers to recycle cooling water rather than consume it once-through.
Mandated water-use reporting to the Department of Natural Resources.
Utility-rate provisions aimed to keep data center infrastructure costs off household bills.

timeline.milestone: Died at end of 2025-26 session without Senate passage
timeline.detail: Date approximate — re-verify adjournment disposition

bills.title: An Act to Establish the Maine Data Center Coordination Council and Place a Temporary Limitation on Certain Data Centers
bills.sponsor: Rep. Drew Gattine (D-Westbrook)
bills.summary: Would have imposed a moratorium on municipal and state permitting of data centers with loads of 20 MW or more until November 1, 2027 while a new Data Center Coordination Council studied impacts including water and energy infrastructure demands. Vetoed by Gov. Mills, who said she would have signed it with an exemption for the Androscoggin Mill project in Jay that reuses existing water infrastructure.
bills.status_detail: Vetoed April 24, 2026; House sustained the veto April 29, 2026 (override fell short of two-thirds). Verified on mainelegislature.org bill status.

recent_news.title: Governor Mills Announces Decision on LD 307
recent_news.source: Office of Governor Janet T. Mills
recent_news.takeaway: Mills vetoed the near-first-in-nation statewide moratorium, citing the Jay mill redevelopment that reuses existing water and electrical infrastructure.

recent_news.title: Maine Governor Vetoes First-in-Nation Data Center Moratorium Bill, Greenlights Rural Development
recent_news.takeaway: The veto is read industry-wide as a near-miss showing statewide moratoriums are now politically viable.

bills.public_sentiment: Environmental and community groups strongly supported the pause; the governor and rural development interests opposed it as written, specifically to protect the Androscoggin Mill data center project. The House override attempt failed on Veto Day.

general_principles.note: Would have paused all state and municipal permitting of 20+ MW data centers until November 2027.
Created a Data Center Coordination Council to study resource impacts before further build-out.
Tied resumption of permitting to completion of a coordinated state review framework.

bills.title: One-Year Moratorium on New Data Center Zoning Permits and Site Development Plans
bills.sponsor: Denver City Council (unanimous)
bills.summary: Pauses acceptance and processing of new zoning permits and site development plans for data centers in the City and County of Denver for one year while the city drafts rules on water consumption, energy use, noise, and siting — adopted amid Denver Water's call for a 20% drought reduction and a proposed CoreSite facility estimated at ~235,000 gallons/day.
bills.status_detail: Passed unanimously by Denver City Council May 18, 2026; effective May 21, 2026; expires May 2027 unless extended. Confirmed via Denver Legistar council bill text and multiple news reports.

recent_news.title: Data center moratorium gets unanimous approval in Denver, but that's just the beginning
recent_news.takeaway: Council passed the pause unanimously and launched a working group to write permanent water, energy, noise, and siting rules.

recent_news.title: Denver proposes yearlong moratorium on new data centers
recent_news.takeaway: The proposal emerged directly after Colorado's statewide data center water bills stalled, with water use a primary stated driver.

bills.public_sentiment: Neighborhood groups and water-conservation advocates strongly supported it, galvanized by the CoreSite facility's projected 86 million gallons/year during Stage 1 drought; data center developers and some business groups warned it pushes investment to neighboring jurisdictions.

general_principles.note: One-year citywide pause on new data center zoning permits and site development plans.
Working group must assess impacts and craft water/energy/noise/siting regulations before permitting resumes.
Explicitly motivated by Denver Water's 20% drought-reduction target and data center water demand.

bills.title: Data center water and energy use reporting and tariff requirements
bills.sponsor: House Committee on Commerce
bills.summary: Requires data centers to file quarterly water-use reports with the Iowa DNR (volume, source, and efficiency) and quarterly energy reports with the Iowa Utilities Commission, with the reported information posted publicly online within 30 days; also requires a separate electric tariff so data-center costs are not shifted onto other ratepayers.
bills.status_detail: Introduced in the 2026 session (91st General Assembly) as a committee bill from the House Committee on Commerce; a more comprehensive successor to the earlier HF 2447 reporting bill. Bill text confirmed on legis.iowa.gov; final session disposition not re-checked — re-verify before relying.

bills.title: Eliminating data center tax incentives and adding clean-energy and sustainability conditions
bills.sponsor: Energy and Technology Committee
bills.summary: Would have repealed Connecticut's data-center tax incentives (PA 21-1) and conditioned data centers on meeting the state's clean-electricity standard (100% clean by 2040), paying prevailing wage, and meeting a sustainable-design / green-building standard; framed by the committee around data centers' water and energy use.

bills.title: Data center ratepayer protections, reclaimed-water cooling, and local authority
bills.sponsor: Sen. Jay Collins
bills.summary: Bars utilities from passing large-scale data-center electricity and infrastructure costs onto residential/small-business ratepayers and requires 50+ MW users to pay their full cost of service; requires data centers using at least 100,000 gallons/day to use reclaimed water for cooling when environmentally, economically, and technically feasible; requires public discussion of water/utility impacts before approval and preserves local governments' zoning/denial authority; tightens aquifer withdrawal permitting.
bills.status_detail: Signed by Gov. DeSantis May 7, 2026 at Florida Polytechnic University; passed Senate 37-0 and House 92-16 with a final 31-6 Senate concurrence vote. Effective July 1, 2026. Verified via flgov.com press release and flsenate.gov bill history.

recent_news.takeaway: Signing announcement frames the bill primarily as ratepayer protection, with reclaimed-water cooling and local zoning authority as companion provisions.

recent_news.takeaway: Trade-press summary confirms the 100,000 gal/day reclaimed-water threshold and that local governments retain approval authority over major developments.

bills.public_sentiment: Broad bipartisan support (37-0 Senate, 92-16 House) framed around protecting ratepayers from subsidizing Big Tech infrastructure; environmental and open-government advocates flagged during committee that the 'feasible' reclaimed-water standard leaves an implementation gap, since utilities and operators determine feasibility with limited independent review.

general_principles.note: Prohibits shifting large-load electricity/infrastructure costs onto residential and small-business ratepayers; requires 50+ MW users to pay full cost of service.
Requires reclaimed water for cooling at 100,000+ gal/day facilities where feasible, aimed at reducing potable/aquifer draw.
Tightens aquifer withdrawal permitting and preserves local governments' zoning/denial authority over hyperscale projects.

bills.title: Accelerating Federal Permitting of Data Center Infrastructure
bills.sponsor: President Trump (Executive Order 14318, 90 FR 142)
bills.summary: Directs the Army Corps to identify or develop a data-center-specific nationwide permit under CWA §404 and Rivers and Harbors Act §10, establishes NEPA categorical exclusions for data-center infrastructure, provides for programmatic ESA §7 consultation covering multi-year construction windows, and expands FAST-41 coverage to qualifying data centers. Sets the >100 MW 'Data Center Project' and $500M / national-security 'Qualifying Project' thresholds the implementing actions key off.
bills.status_detail: Signed 2025-07-23; in force and substantially implemented — the Army Corps' 2026 reissuance of Nationwide Permit 39 expressly enumerating data centers is the §404 directive carried out. NB: the order reaches §404 dredge-and-fill and RHA §10 only; it contains no NPDES (§402) directive, so operational discharge permitting is untouched by it.

general_principles.note: The defining federal instrument on the deregulatory side: it directs agencies to find faster §404/§10 pathways for data centers rather than to condition them.
Centralizes data-center permitting through FAST-41 and programmatic consultations instead of project-by-project review.

timeline.detail: Issued alongside America's AI Action Plan; published at 90 FR 142
QTS Richmond Technology Park DC5 becomes the first data center covered

bills.sponsor: White House Office of Science and Technology Policy
bills.summary: The policy blueprint EO 14318 implements. Calls for a data-center-tailored Clean Water Act §404 nationwide permit, new NEPA categorical exclusions, FAST-41 expansion, and streamlining or reduction of Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act and CERCLA requirements for AI infrastructure.
bills.status_detail: Released 2025-07-23, the same day as EO 14318. A blueprint rather than a legal instrument — it binds nobody directly, but it is the stated source of the §404 and FAST-41 directives that do.

general_principles.note: Names the CWA, CAA and CERCLA as burdens to reduce for AI infrastructure — the clearest statement of the federal posture.

bills.title: Temporary Moratorium on Data Centers While the State Develops Standards
bills.sponsor: Gov. Kathy Hochul
bills.summary: One-year pause on DEC discretionary permits for data centers at or above 50 MW. Orders the Department of Public Service to report on data-center impacts including water use and water quality, and directs DEC to assess within 12 months whether the state's water-withdrawal program needs new rules for very large users.
bills.status_detail: Signed 2026-07-14; in force. This — not the tracked NY S10642/A11560 — is the instrument that actually imposed New York's moratorium. The Governor neither signed nor vetoed the bill; she superseded it with an executive order at a higher threshold (50 MW vs the bill's 20 MW), which is a materially narrower pause than the bill would have imposed.

general_principles.note: First statewide data-center moratorium actually in effect anywhere in the US.
Pauses DEC discretionary permitting rather than banning construction outright.
Orders the DEC water-withdrawal-program assessment and the DPS impact report before standards are set.

bills.bill_id: TX PUC Energy and Water Use Survey (data centers)
bills.title: PUCT / TWDB energy and water use survey for data centers and crypto mining
bills.sponsor: Public Utility Commission of Texas with the Texas Water Development Board
bills.summary: A survey directed by the Legislature in the 2025 budget, collecting electricity and water use from data centers and virtual-currency mining facilities. The only water-specific utility-commission action found nationally — the marquee data-center rate dockets elsewhere (PUCO 24-508-EL-ATA, the Georgia PSC large-load tariff, Dominion's SCC proceedings) are energy-only and carry no water provisions.
bills.status_detail: Open and voluntary, with response rates the Legislature has called inadequate: about a third of surveyed data centers responded in 2024 and 17% in 2025; the most recent round drew 28 companies covering 92 facilities. PUCT reopened the survey 2026-07-01 with responses due 2026-07-10. The Texas Water Development Board's own water-consumption surveys have been mandatory since 2023. Watch for a mandatory PUCT/ERCOT registration requirement replacing the voluntary survey.

general_principles.note: Asks for facility-level water use directly from operators rather than through utilities.
The instructive failure in this dataset: a disclosure mechanism with no compulsion produced a 17% response rate.
